client: I've been having a really hard time at work lately, and honestly I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything. There's this colleague, Jessica, who keeps presenting my ideas in meetings like they're her own, and my manager doesn't seem to notice or care. It's making me feel invisible, like my job could just disappear and nobody would even register that I was contributing anything.
therapist: It sounds really demoralizing to feel like your contributions are going unseen, especially when someone else is actively taking credit for your work — that sense of invisibility can quietly chip away at your confidence and sense of purpose. I also hear a little skepticism about whether talking will help, and I want you to know that's a completely valid feeling to bring into this space. I'm curious — when you imagine your manager *does* notice your work, what does that picture look like, and what do you think gets in the way of that happening right now?

client: Honestly, when I imagine my manager actually noticing my work, I picture her stopping by my desk and just... acknowledging that the project went well because of what I did, not because of Derek. But then I immediately think, why would that ever happen when Derek is so loud and confident in meetings and I just kind of sit there hoping someone will connect the dots on their own. I guess what gets in the way is that I don't speak up, but every time I think about doing that, I feel this knot in my stomach like I'll come across as desperate or braggy.
therapist: It's really insightful that you've already identified the pattern — that speaking up feels risky because of this fear of being seen as "desperate or braggy," so instead you wait and hope, and then feel invisible when the dots don't get connected. That fear makes a lot of sense, but I'd gently invite you to examine it a little: when you picture a colleague confidently sharing their contributions, do you actually see them as braggy, or do you see them as someone who owns their work? What do you think that double standard — the one you apply to yourself but not others — might be telling you?

client: Okay, when I picture someone else speaking up in a meeting, I don't think "ugh, they're so braggy" — I actually do respect it, like they know what they're doing and they're not apologizing for it. But when I imagine doing the same thing myself, it just feels... different, like the rules change for me somehow. I guess that double standard is telling me I don't really believe I deserve to take up that space the way other people do.
therapist: That's a really meaningful insight — recognizing that you hold yourself to a harsher standard than everyone else is often one of the first cracks of light in changing a long-held belief. That core sense of "I don't deserve to take up space" didn't appear out of nowhere, and it's worth being curious about rather than just accepting as fact. Where do you think that belief first took root for you — is it something you can trace back to earlier experiences, or does it feel like it's always just been there?

client: I think it goes back pretty far, honestly. I remember being a kid and feeling like I was always in the way, like my needs were kind of an inconvenience to everyone around me. It wasn't anything dramatic, no big single event, just this slow accumulation of moments where I learned to make myself smaller so things would go more smoothly.
therapist: There's something quietly profound about what you just described — not one dramatic moment, but a slow, steady lesson that shrinking yourself was how you kept the peace, and over time that became just... who you believed you were supposed to be. That kind of learning runs deep precisely because it felt so normal, so unremarkable, even as it was shaping something really fundamental about how you move through the world. I'm wondering — now that you can see that younger version of you who learned to make themselves smaller, what do you think she actually needed to hear back then?

client: I think she needed someone to tell her that her needs weren't a burden, that it was okay to take up space. But even saying that out loud feels kind of hollow, like I know it intellectually but it doesn't really land anywhere inside me. It's like the words make sense but they don't reach whatever part of me still believes the opposite.
therapist: That gap you're describing — between knowing something in your head and truly *feeling* it — is one of the most honest and common experiences people have in this kind of work, and it doesn't mean you're broken or that change isn't possible. The part of you that still believes you're a burden has had decades of practice, so it makes sense it won't simply step aside because the logical mind says so. I'm curious — are there any moments, even small or fleeting ones, where you've actually *felt* like your presence mattered to someone, where it landed somewhere deeper than just a thought?

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to say no, not really. But there was this one moment a few weeks ago where my friend texted me out of nowhere just to say she was thinking about me, and for like a split second it felt warm, real, not just something I brushed off. Then almost immediately I started wondering if she was just being polite, and the feeling kind of collapsed on itself.
therapist: That moment with your friend is actually really significant — your heart *did* receive it, even if just for a split second, which tells us that the capacity to feel like you matter is still alive in you, even if it gets quickly overridden. What's so telling is that your mind almost immediately reached for a way to explain the warmth away, turning "she cares about me" into "she's probably just being polite" — that's the old belief protecting itself. What do you think would have to be true for you to let that moment of warmth just... stay, without needing to dismantle it?

client: I don't know... I guess part of me would have to actually believe that I'm worth caring about without needing a reason attached to it. But that feels really far away, like it's this abstract thing people say but I can't quite grasp what it would feel like in my body. And honestly, even talking about it right now makes me a little anxious, like I'm setting myself up to be disappointed if I let myself believe it and then it turns out I was wrong.
therapist: There's something really tender and brave about what you just named — that believing you're worth caring about feels both out of reach *and* dangerous, like hope itself is a risk. That anxiety makes complete sense: if you've spent a lifetime bracing for the message that your needs are too much, then opening the door to "maybe I matter" feels like stepping onto uncertain ground. I want to sit with that for a moment — what's the worst thing you imagine happening if you let yourself believe it, even just a little, and it turned out to be true?

client: I think the worst thing would be that I'd start to relax, let my guard down, and then something would happen to prove I was wrong all along. Like, if I actually let myself believe I matter to someone and then they leave or pull away, that would hurt so much more than if I'd never believed it in the first place. It's almost safer to stay in this low-grade loneliness than to risk that kind of crash.
therapist: What you're describing is such a deeply human protection strategy — staying in the low-grade loneliness feels like *control*, like you're choosing the pain on your own terms rather than risking a much bigger one. But I want to gently reflect something back to you: the crash you're so afraid of is hypothetical, while the loneliness you're describing is already here, already costing you something every day. I wonder — if the pain of staying guarded and the pain of potential loss both hurt, what might make the risk of connection worth it, even just a little?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right that the loneliness is already real and already hurts. But when you ask what might make the risk worth it, my mind just goes blank, like I genuinely can't picture a version of closeness that doesn't eventually end in me feeling worse than I do now. I guess I've just been burned enough times that the hypothetical loss doesn't feel hypothetical to me at all — it feels like a certainty I'm just postponing.
therapist: What you're describing isn't just a fear — it's a conclusion you've already reached based on real experiences of being hurt, which makes it feel less like a possibility and more like a law of nature that you'd be foolish to argue with. That's not pessimism, that's your nervous system trying to protect you using the only evidence it's ever been given. I'm curious — when you think about those times you were burned, were there also moments of genuine connection before the loss, and if so, do you think those moments had any value, even knowing how they ended?

client: Yeah, there were moments... I remember laughing with someone until my sides hurt, feeling like they actually got me for once. And I guess those moments felt real at the time, maybe even worth something. But then when it all fell apart, it was like those good memories almost made it worse, like they became evidence of what I'd lost rather than something I got to keep.
therapist: There's something really poignant in what you just said — that the good memories became evidence of loss rather than something that belonged to you, something no one could take back. But I want to gently offer a reframe: those moments of laughing until your sides hurt, of feeling truly *gotten* — they happened, they were real, and they lived in you before the loss and still live in you now as you describe them. What if those memories aren't proof that connection always ends in pain, but proof that you are actually capable of receiving it — that the warmth did land, that you do know what it feels like to matter to someone?
